name: Phase Three: Set Up Governance
title: Phase Three: Set Up Governance
answer: Phase Three: Set Up Governance means completing the school's approval, privacy, ownership and family notice steps before any student uses an AI tool in a pilot. It matters because skipping these steps creates confusion about data, weakens trust with families and can block later scaling if agreements are missing. The book treats this as a short investment that prevents long cleanup.

sections.body: This idea is the governance work that must be finished before a pilot begins. The tool is placed on the approved list with its limits recorded, and a data privacy agreement is signed when student information is involved. One person is named to own the pilot and report its results, so responsibility does not float between staff. Families of participating students receive a short and plain notice about what the tool does and whom to contact with questions. The problem it solves is the common habit of rushing a pilot because a teacher is eager or the school year is short, which leaves the school unable to answer basic questions later.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school or classroom, the practice starts before any student touches the tool. Leaders confirm the governance steps from Chapter 3 are complete, add the tool to the approved list with limits noted, and sign a data privacy agreement if student information is involved. They name one owner for the pilot who reports results, and they send families a short, plain notice explaining the tool and giving a contact for questions. The text does not give grade bands for this phase, so the same sequence applies wherever the pilot runs. Parent education also belongs here, through a short evening session or a one page guide on how the school uses AI, what the pilot will test and how families can help at home.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The supplied text gives no study, figure or evidence label for this idea. It argues from practice and from the costs of skipping governance, such as a parent asking what data the tool collected when nobody knows, or a district wanting to scale and finding the vendor will not sign the needed agreement. It also states that a week spent on governance up front saves months of cleanup afterward. On that basis, this idea rests on practice rather than research.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits and risks are that pilots often cut corners, usually when a teacher is excited and the school year is short. Skipping governance can leave the school unable to explain what data was collected, and it can stop a successful pilot from scaling if the vendor will not sign the required agreement. Families who learn about the pilot from their child tend to worry, while families who understand its purpose tend to support it even when they have concerns. The decisions that stay with people include completing the Chapter 3 governance steps, setting the approved list and its limits, signing the privacy agreement when student information is involved, naming the pilot owner, reporting results, sending the family notice and providing parent education. The tool does not make those decisions.
